1817856,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.35,1955-07-18,eb20cb84-344e-40aa-b7af-f2a7ff88f1f5,ca.m.9512,Mr. Castleden:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,Mr. Chairman, in the remarks I was making prior to the lunch hour I was referring to the fact that in some instances the veteran in Canada is having some difficulty under the legislation, and recommended that since the government's responsibility had increased, it should assume the responsibility of making it possible for the veteran under the allowances to live decently and well. I was going to sum up my remarks by going over the recommendations made to the minister and making one or two suggestions which I think would help the situation a great deal.

As a member of the cabinet the minister should see, I think, if something could not be done by the government in its fiscal policy to lower the cost of living in this country for those people who are depending upon pensions. It would help Canada in many ways. I merely suggest to the minister that in his position as a cabinet minister he could help Canadians in this field of life and in other lines of endeavour to subsist.

There is one feature of this whole war veterans allowance set-up which I think will appeal particularly to the minister. I refer to the recipient of the war veterans allowance who is receiving the maximum of permissive income of $1,440. I do not know how he and his family can live with the cost of living as it is today. Supposing that man

becomes eligible to receive the old age pension of $40 per month which would come to him automatically on reaching the age of 70 years. Under the regulations as they exist today he would not receive that $40 per month.

I do not know of any other person in Canada who is penalized to that extent. The lowest wage earner and the wealthiest person in Canada under the regulations as they exist today are eligible to receive this additional $40 per month upon reaching the age of 70 years. I think it is an excellent move; I think Canada can be proud of it, but Canada cannot be proud of the fact that the recipients of war veterans allowances are denied the right to this extra $40 per month. The pay and allowances of the Prime Minister amount to $37,000 per year, but on reaching the age of 70 he received the old age pension of $40 per month. But the war veterans allowance recipient does not receive that extra $40 on reaching age 70.

I think this is one piece of discrimination which is not good for Canada, and I should like to see it removed. I think it would be good for Canada, I think it would be good for parliament, I think it would particularly raise the esteem of Canadians for the administration of this department if the minister would see to this. I am sure he would receive the general support of this house and the people generally if he would raise the permissive income or the war veterans allowance for a married veteran to $120 from the $108 it is at present, under today's cost of living.

Finally I repeat the suggestion that has been made that a standing committee of veterans of this house or a standing committee of this house on veterans affairs be set up which would receive representations from veterans organizations, veterans widows organizations, imperial veterans organizations and so on.

That committee could then make recommendations to this house based on those requests, and the necessary legislation could be placed on the statute books of this country and do much to relieve the situation confronting these people who deserve everything that Canada can give them.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,George Hugh Castleden,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=eb20cb84-344e-40aa-b7af-f2a7ff88f1f5&Language=E&Section=ALL
1817857,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.36,1955-07-18,043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6,ca.m.6101,Mr. Nicholson:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with what has been said by other hon. members about the staff of this department. I appreciate what the member for Kootenay West has said about the new building, and when the minister rises I should like him to tell the committee how many hours have been lost this summer as a result of that heat. What would be that loss as represented in dollars and cents?

The question of war veterans allowance has been covered at considerable length but in view of letters which have come to me from Legion branches in my area I would not feel justified in letting these estimates pass without urging upon the minister to use his best efforts to have the government reconsider the matter. When the minister discussed the matter on March 4 he said that under the request of the Legion, which would increase the permissive income of single persons, they would be placed in as favourable a position as a veteran who had an 80 per cent disability pension, and if the permissive income of a married veteran were increased to $2,000 he would be receiving nearly as much as a 100 per cent disability married man, who would receive $2,040.

That is a good argument but I suggest that it would be a better argument to ask that the whole pension schedule be increased. I saw a cartoon in a newspaper recently showing a prisoner in the dock congratulating the judge upon having received an increase of $50 a week. The Minister of Justice has provided that increase for some of his personnel, the judges. All the veteran is asking is an allowance of $1,200 a year or $100 a month, with $2,000 for the married veteran. On March 4 the minister said that he believed that the new allowances are capable of allowing the recipient to maintain a reasonable level of subsistence. I was not too sure of the meaning of that word and I found in the dictionary that to subsist means to exist, to continue to exist, to remain in being, to keep oneself alive, to support life. Possibly it is enough to keep oneself alive, but surely the people of Canada do not want to grind down this section of our people so that they merely can subsist. The Canadian Legion asks that the permissive ceiling be raised to $100 per month for single persons and $2,000 for married persons. Surely this is a very modest and reasonable request. I hope that, before parliament meets next year, the minister will be able to convince his colleagues that the extra $13 million he estimated might be necessary can be voted without any question. Last week we voted $170 million for mutual aid as part of our national defence program, which totalled nearly $2 billion. Surely, if we can vote money on this scale, the $13 million the minister estimated would be necessary, if the request of the Canadian Legion were met, can be found by the cabinet.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Alexander Malcolm Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6&Language=E&Section=ALL
1817858,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.37,1955-07-18,03bdeb92-5e2c-42ef-87e7-af2178b73f74,ca.m.2134,Mr. Patterson:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,Mr. Chairman, I am sure the veterans of Canada are quite pleased with the pattern of legislation which obtains in Canada at the present time. However, as the hon. member for Acadia stated this
Supply-Veterans Affairs

morning, there are still some loose ends that need to be taken care of. I should like to refer very briefly this afternoon to two matters, because I feel that they are two of those loose ends that certainly need to be tied up.

The matter of the ceiling allowed for permissive income is of great concern to the war veterans, and I am thinking especially of those who are the recipients of the war veterans allowances and who are not able to supplement their incomes by casual earnings. It may be because they are not physically able to do so, or it may be because economic conditions in their particular localities do not allow them that opportunity.

I think that this matter should be taken under careful advisement and something further done in this connection. There are those on war veterans allowances, to whom I have referred, and there are those who receive small superannuation allowances and disability pensions. As the hon. member for Yorkton mentioned a short time ago, they are not allowed to receive the full benefit of their pension, whatever it may be, and the allowances. In view of the fact that those who are able can now supplement their income to a fairly satisfactory total, these other groups should be given careful consideration. Even with the increases in allowances that have been granted, it is still inadequate to meet the cost of living at the present time. So I would request that the minister take another look at that particular situation and as soon as possible bring in some further legislation that will take care of it.

There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer this afternoon. It is the delay in the processing of appeals for pensions. Last fall I had the opportunity of meeting the representatives of the Legion branches in my own riding, and this is one of the matters that were brought to my attention. It was felt that in some cases the delay is rather lengthy, and they were of the opinion that when pensions are granted they should be made retroactive to the date of application. In the minutes of the proceedings and evidence of the special committee on veterans affairs of this present session, on pages 11 and 12, this matter was referred to by the dominion president of the Canadian Legion. I am not going to take the time to read these particular sections, but they refer to this matter of making the pensions retroactive. It may be the fault of the department, or there may be other factors that enter into it, but certainly there should be the possibility of making these pensions retroactive to the date of application rather than the date on which they are granted.

That would remove some of the causes of dissatisfaction among the veterans of Canada, because they would realize that this is another way in which the minister is endeavouring to take care of their particular problems.

These are the two matters I wished to raise this afternoon. I concur, of course, in many of the other matters that have been raised -other matters of legislation that could be attended to-but I just wish to emphasize these two at this moment.

1817859,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.38,1955-07-18,2b02ca65-52af-436d-9739-c9565c0af670,ca.m.2430,Mr. Lapointe:,Minister of Veterans Affairs,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention at this stage of the discussion on item 1 to make any lengthy remarks, but I should like to refer to some of the statements made by hon. members during the course of the debate this morning. I should like to thank all members who have participated in the debate for the ideas they have put forward, for the criticism they have offered and for the suggestions which have been advanced.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, who started the debate, expressed some regrets that the minister did not make, at the opening of the discussion on the first item of the estimates, any extensive statement. He said that he thought the veterans of Canada would be interested in having the minister's views on the various problems. Well, the veterans of Canada are afforded the opportunity of having the minister's views on all the problems relating to veterans on many occasions. The minister does meet with the veterans organizations, and the department sees that all veterans are very much made aware of the government's policy and their rights under the existing veterans legislation.

Personally I think that the veterans of Canada are much more interested in legislative action than they are in reading any Hansard statements by the minister. That is what I have endeavoured to do during the five years I have presided over the department, as referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I have endeavoured to do so, and I think the statute books of Canada show that these efforts have not been in vain and that every phase of veterans legislation that existed in the statute books of Canada when I took over this office has been amended in order to meet the changing circumstances as they have arisen. The pension legislation has been amended and at times rates have been increased; war veterans allowances have been increased on two occasions; treatment regulations have been amended to make them more generous; the Veterans Land Act has been amended to enlarge the scope of the act as it was originally conceived. This has been done without

the necessity of making any extensive statements in the house. However, the results are there and the fact that they are there shows that this continuing attention and consideration, which the hon. member has urged and which rightly must be given to all veterans problems, does exist in the department at the present time.

As I listened to the remarks made by hon. members, it occurred to me that little that had not been discussed before was advanced during this discussion. That is simply normal procedure because, as was pointed out, this year we had a special committee on veterans affairs which studied the legislation concerning war veterans allowance and the department's estimates were thoroughly scrutinized by the special committee on estimates. I would therefore say that practically all aspects of veterans legislation were considered and discussed by the members of those respective committees.

Hon. members have again urged the establishment of a standing committee on veterans affairs. May I say that, to my knowledge, not only during the five years during which I have held this portfolio but during the time of my predecessor similar representations were made, and the policy of the government was expressed at that time. I have repeated it on various occasions. The government sets up a special veterans affairs committee on every occasion when any major changes are to be made in the veterans legislation in order that these changes and amendments can be thoroughly discussed by members of that committee. On those occasions all veterans organizations that wish to make representations before the committee are afforded the opportunity to do so; and they have always taken advantage of that opportunity. I think hon. members will bear me out in this statement. Regardless of the terms of reference of that committee, the veterans organizations have come forward and have been permitted to express their views on every matter. The proof of that statement lies in this fact. Even though the last committee this session was set up to study the war veterans allowance, during the course of the debate this morning some hon. members quoted from briefs of veterans organizations certain extracts which referred not to the war veterans allowance but rather to some other aspect of veterans legislation.

Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, as hon. members are aware, these veterans organizations such as the Legion every year present a brief to the cabinet. They are permitted to come here, put forward their views, express their ideas and discuss with the cabinet and with

the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs all their problems. To say that the mere fact of establishing a standing committee on veterans affairs would permit these veterans groups more easily to express their views is to disregard the situation as it exists now. I pointed out-I think it was last year when a similar change was asked-that a special committee of this house had been set up to examine the procedure of this House of Commons and to recommend the changes which this committee found to be desirable.

I only wish now to point out that the report of this committee, which was a unanimous one, was brought down a short time ago and that in this report no reference was made to a standing committee on veterans affairs.

Many of those who have spoken have referred, during the course of their remarks, to the legislation on war veterans allowance. During the course of this session we had some quite lengthy debates on war veterans allowance. Extensive changes were proposed with regard to the legislation. The changes were referred to the special committee on veterans affairs, were reported to this house and were adopted. I do not know that I can add much to the remarks that I made at that time and those which my parliamentary assistant made during the course of the debate in this house. Again we were urged to admit under war veterans allowance those men who served during world war I in the United Kingdom only. I think this matter has been thoroughly discussed on many occasions previously. I think it was generally accepted that war veterans allowance was paid to a man who had had front-line service. In order to compensate for the hardships which he had suffered there, he was permitted to draw what was originally the equivalent of the old age pension some ten years before any other Canadian citizen could do so, on the ground that he had pre-aged by that number of years. During the course of the debates and the discussions that took place in previous sessions before I introduced new legislation this year, one of the strongest arguments for an increase in rates made by those who are now asking that service in England during world war I be recognized for the purpose of war veterans allowance was that every recipient had front-line service. I can remember the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra speaking with much force on that subject and many of us were inclined to share his views. But how can you use the same argument when it comes to service in England during the first world war? It is true that service in England during the second world war qualified a veteran for war veterans allowance but that was because during the second war,
Supply-Veterans Affairs
owing to the change in the character of the war, England was considered as a theatre of war whereas it was not so considered during the first war.

Some representations have been made that war veterans allowance should be paid to men who would otherwise qualify but who cannot qualify because of the fact that they reside outside of Canada; or again it is urged that the recipient of war veterans allowance should be permitted, by reason of health considerations, to live outside of Canada. Leaving aside the merit of the question itself, I think hon. members will realize that such a provision would bring about a serious administrative problem. As a matter of fact, if anyone is interested and goes back to the original discussion before 1930 when the war veterans allowance legislation was first introduced, one finds that the various veterans groups at that time endorsed the policy that it should not be paid outside of Canada. Of course, I admit that circumstances have changed, and certainly the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Kootenay West deserves consideration. We are looking into it at the present time.

1817861,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.40,1955-07-18,2b02ca65-52af-436d-9739-c9565c0af670,ca.m.2430,Mr. Lapointe:,Minister of Veterans Affairs,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,I would not like to go into any detail on the question of the permissive income under the War Veterans Allowance Act. He brought this matter before the special committee on estimates when the departmental estimates were before that committee. The rate is determined by the prevailing rates for similar work in private employment in that locality. This department does not determine the wage rates that will be paid to prevailing rate employees. We simply pay the rate which we are instructed to pay. The rate is determined by a survey made by the Department of Labour at regular intervals.

The same situation exists amongst these prevailing rate employees as exists amongst the tradesmen all over Canada. As hon. members are fully aware, the various tradesmen such as carpenters, electricians or plumbers, are not paid the same rates all over Canada. The wage rates of these people vary, depending on the locality in which they live. A similar situation exists with regard to the prevailing rate employees in this department.

The hon. member for Selkirk also wanted assurance that the leniency the officials of my department said they would exercise with regard to some of his constituents established under the Veterans Land Act, and who had no crop last year, would be exercised. I can assure my hon friend that it is not, and has never been, the policy of the department to dispossess or otherwise prosecute any of our settlers under this act. As a matter of fact, the great success achieved by the Veterans Land Act since 1945 has been due to the close co-operation which has existed between the settlers, the departmental officials and the settlement officers who visit them to help them along. As a result, the figures which were given before the estimates committee indicate we have a splendid record under the Veterans Land Act, not only as to the establishment of good, stable settlers, but so far as collection is concerned. This we intend to continue, as we want to keep these men on the land.

While the hon. member for Acadia did make some remarks which I have already covered, he asked whether classes one to eleven pensioners, hospitalized in a departmental institution, are charged the same rates as other veterans under section 13. He referred to the pamphlet issued by the department explaining the operation of section 13. The answer is that they pay the same rates, but that, in computing their adjusted income, 25 per cent of their pension is exempted. He referred also to the fact that 100 per cent pensioners who were hospitalized had $15 deducted from their pension, as other pensioners did. He pointed out the fact that whereas a low disability pensioner did not actually have a deduction, his pension was raised to the equivalent of 85 per cent, and it was the high pensioner who did suffer from

I can answer only by stating again what the formula is. I think hon. members will agree that it is very simple. The assessment formula for a farmer under the War Veterans Allowance Act is as follows:

1817886,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.65,1955-07-18,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. Gillis:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. This question of treatment for non-recognized disability is a pretty serious one to the older veterans. Judging from conversations I had recently with some older veterans who had been in the hospital and found themselves in the circumstances that we are describing, there does not seem to have been much change in the regulations in the last year.

Take the veteran of the first war. He has a 20 to 25 per cent pension for a gunshot wound. There may be other conditions, but that is the recognized disability. He is in hospital for that disability and he is of the age when he is running into other trouble, kidneys, prostate, and minor operations which might be necessary. Those things could be fixed up within a few days without any great cost while he is in the hospital,

but when he brings these disabilities to the attention of the doctor he is immediately taken off pay and allowances and his income is assessed as to what he made last year. Unless he is willing to pay the $9.50 per day the condition is not touched.

A veteran of the first world war on pension finds that his pension is pretty well fixed today. If he is getting 25 per cent today that is it as far as that disability is concerned. I cannot see why there should not be more flexibility in the administration of these regulations. Greater latitude should be given to the superintendent of a hospital in connection with men who are in for pensionable disabilities and who find they have other troubles that need to be taken care of. More attention should be paid to these men without the rigidity there appears to be today in the regulations.

It is one thing for us to talk about regulations but it is another thing when those regulations are applied. I am led to believe that there is not much flexibility in this particular matter today, any more than there was two years ago. I should like the minister to make a check on this.

I think the emphasis in connection with veterans legislation is changing today from what it was a couple of years ago. At that time it was a question of getting the pension and veterans allowance rates increased, but the matter of treatment is the main emphasis today. Veterans of the last war are beginning to discover more and more troubles, and this is where the rigidity is creeping into the legislation in and around the hospitals. I think we will have to take a better look at this whole matter of treatment.

Let me say to the minister that I think the application of veterans legislation was 100 per cent more flexible 20 years ago than it is today. It is only within the last five years that this kind of thing has begun to tighten up. Hardship is being created. It looks to me as though we are getting back to the days when we said to these men, ""The war is over; we do not need you any more."" It is all right to pass legislation, but the real test of any legislation is the way it is administered. We did not pass this legislation merely to make jobs. 1817901,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.80,1955-07-18,d2512bc7-c1b4-48ab-9772-1abe28ea07fa,ca.m.1774,Mr. Churchill:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,The more people who call ""carried"", the longer I shall talk. We ran into that when we were in the committee on estimates. It is not helpful at all to those of us who are attempting to get information.
The number of veterans on war veterans allowance is shown as 25,038 in the last departmental report. We received the information-I think it was in the estimates

committee-that the applications for war veterans allowances in the year 1953-54 were numerous and resulted in approval being granted to 83'6 per cent of the applicants. I draw that to the attention of the minister as being in sharp contrast with the number of applications that come before the pension commission and are rejected, as I hope to point out later on when we come to that particular item.

I should like to say a word in regard to what the minister said concerning treating England as a theatre of war for first world war veterans. I had not given any particular attention to that until this year. I notice that some arguments in this connection have been advanced at various times, and the special committee on veterans affairs discussed this particular problem. It arises, as the minister has said, because the United Kingdom has been declared a theatre of war for the world war II people. Once that was done, it was only natural that people who served in England in the first world war would wonder why they were prevented from coming under this particular section of the act. Until you look into the matter, on the face of it you think they should not be admitted, but I feel a second look is perhaps necessary.

As the minister pointed out, in its origin the war veterans allowance was for people who served in a theatre of war. He mentioned ""front line service"", but a theatre of war does not necessarily involve front line service. In the first world war England was not considered a theatre of war. But when you compare the two, it is a little difficult for the veteran of world war I who was in England for a while to find that the world war II veteran who served only in England in that way becomes eligible for war veterans allowance. I think it is deserving of further study.

When hon. members were discussing this in the special committee the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich asked for information as to the men who had reached England in 1914 and 1915, as contrasted with those who got there very late, say in 1918. Those figures apparently were not available, but I think this is a matter that requires a little further study and should not be simply brushed off. I noted that when this was being discussed by that committee, one of the officials estimated that if the United Kingdom were declared a theatre of war for the first world war veterans, there would be 52,000 still living whose services was restricted to the United Kingdom. Of that number he estimated that 11,500 would be eligible for war veterans allowances, which is 22 per cent, and that the cost would be $9,650,000.

Well, I question those figures. I have sometimes questioned the minister's figures. He likes to throw millions at us and then we are shocked and stunned and have no argument forthcoming, because it seems too large a matter to deal with. But I rather question these figures. I would suggest that 10 per cent of those who served in England in the first world war might become eligible, not 22 per cent. If you get your percentage from those who are now on war veterans allowances as a percentage of the total survivors of the first world war, as I say there are about 25,000 world war I veterans on war veterans allowances, and that is about 10 per cent of the 240,000 survivors of the first world war who were not disability pensioners. Consequently the figure would be reduced from 11,500 to 5,000, and the cost would be reduced from $9,650,000 to $4,200,000.

Then it should be carried a step further and, if anything is going to be done in regard to the men who were in England in the first world war, some attention will have to be paid, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said, to the time they were there and the year they arrived there. From everything I have ever heard about it, conditions were much worse for the first contingent people on Salisbury plain and those who were there in 1915 than they were in say 1918. I just offer that as a correction of the information which was given to the special committee.

There is one other thing I wish to mention with regard to the war veterans allowance which has been discussed at great length. I think too much emphasis has been placed by the minister on the extension of casual earnings, in that he thereby creates the impression that because the regulations have been eased with regard to casual earnings, people on war veterans allowance are in a much better position. But that situation applies only to a certain number who are in good physical condition and can get casual employment. It does not apply to a great many people who have no other source of income than their war veterans allowance, and who are unable to go out and make these extra dollars that other more physically fit veterans of that age can earn.

I have no intention today of going over the

Supply-Veterans Affairs case at any length, but it seems perfectly clear that the test should be whether the widow had been in Canada for 20 years rather than whether her husband had lived here for 20 years. For example, if the husband died after he had been here 15 years, his widow cannot qualify for the allowance. When the provision was originally made for payment of the war veterans allowance to imperials, the timing was arrived at on the basis that all these imperials had come to Canada by the year 1930.

The minister will remember the discussion which took place in the house session after session about granting the war veterans allowance to imperials. Always it was pointed out-and it was a fact-that all these imperials came here before the year 1930. When the eligibility was granted it just so happened that the law was worded in such a way that rather than taking in those who came here before 1930, it said only those who had been 20 years in the country were eligible. There were a group who had died before they had actually been here for 20 years. Now their widows are just completely out of luck.

I hope the government will take another look at the War Veterans Allowance Act and see whether an amendment cannot be made so as to have the test whether or not the widow has been in Canada for 20 years. Some of these widows are Canadian women who married imperial veterans here, yet they are not eligible because the husband died before he had been 20 years in the country. I think this is an extremely unfair situation, and one which calls for a remedy. There are not a great number involved, but in principle the present law is wrong. These particular widows should be covered. I hope the minister will assure the committee today that the government has not closed the book on this question. I hope it will be possible to have further consideration given to it between now and the next session of the house.

1817909,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.88,1955-07-18,d8888ed2-41ed-4699-b5d8-0cf5d1d35e77,ca.m.51,Mr. Bennett:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,There has not been any change since the committee sat. Casual earnings are taken into consideration with regard to determining the need under the assistance fund. As you know, under the assistance fund the department can pay, in the case of a married man, up to $12 a month-or in other words from $108 to $120, the amount of the permissive income ceiling-and in the case of a single man, the difference between $70 and $80. As I think was announced when the committee was sitting, the assistance fund has been liberalized. There is a better formula, which makes it a better deal for the veteran. It is the intention of the department to use the assistance fund more liberally. But it is true that when the department is taking a look at whether a need exists under the assistance fund, casual earnings are taken into consideration. 1817911,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.90,1955-07-18,d8888ed2-41ed-4699-b5d8-0cf5d1d35e77,ca.m.51,Mr. Bennett:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,I think the big point we made in the committee, if the government did make any point in respect to casual earnings, was that it did not interfere with the rates under the war veterans allowance. We said there were three or four categories of casual earnings which might apply. A veteran could go out and take odd jobs, and that would not affect his rate of allowance. He could take a part-time regular job and earn up to $50 a month, or he could be seasonably employed and he could earn as much as he wished in any 12-week period without affecting his rights. We thought that was a liberal interpretation of casual earnings and I think it was well received throughout the country. It was an important change in administration of the War Veterans Allowance Act.

I cannot elaborate on the assistance fund any more than I have. It is based on need, and a married man may well get along in a small town on $108 per month but he may need $12 more per month if he is living in a city. He may not be able to live on the allowance, and the assistance fund is to meet that need.

Under the assistance fund the department can give him a lump sum payment for fuel, medical bills and so on or, for instance, for a suit of clothes. It is based strictly on need. As I say, we hope the assistance fund is going to be administered more liberally, and there is a better formula than there was.

1817928,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.107,1955-07-18,043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6,ca.m.6101,Mr. Nicholson:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,"I should like to spend a few minutes on this item, Mr. Chairman. I am happy to say that the situation now is quite different from what it was when I came here in 1940. I receive very few complaints from veterans in connection with their dealings with the pension commission. However, I have one case-and I do not know how many there are in Canada like it-which has gone

column2: HOUSE OF

column1: Supply-Veterans Affairs
through the regular channels. The chairman wrote me on April 22 a letter in which appears this closing paragraph:
However in their adjudication they are governed by the provisions of the Pension Act and unfortunately could not concede his claim.
In other words the door appears to be closed in this case.

Very briefly, this veteran is in his seventieth year. He enlisted in 1916 and was wounded in 1917. That is 38 years ago. His regimental number is 782/242. After reviewing the transcript of evidence I wrote Brigadier Topp about a year ago; to be exact it was last October. There are a number of details in the transcript which I think are important.

The veteran took out a life insurance policy for $2,500 in 1922, when he was about to be married. Some ten years later, when applying for pension, he was questioned about this life insurance policy but apparently his answers as they appear in the transcript were rather vague. This veteran tells me that the doctor who examined him was at that time the hon. member for Wood Mountain.

I think most of us have had the experience of having life insurance examinations which have been casual. He got his life insurance policy for $2,500. It seems a pity that 30 years later the fact that he was able to get that policy should be held against him as evidence that he was quite fit at that particular time. The veteran says he was a bit vague, because when he was questioned in 1932 Dr. Donnelly was still living. He says, however, that Dr. Donnelly is now dead and the policy is cancelled, and he does not mind adding that Dr. Donnelly did not even put an instrument on him. The doctor said, ""You appear to be well enough to get a life insurance policy.""

The second piece of information that I think did not receive sufficient attention was that the veteran was able to get the evidence of Dr. Harold, who had examined him in 1917. It is stated at page 25 of the transcript, where Dr. Harold gives evidence, that this man was cleared through the field ambulance *n AuSust>

1917, as a stretcher case, complaining of severe pains and weakness in the back and hips, and possible partial paralysis of the hips. On the first page of the summary of evidence it is stated that there is nothing on the service documents to corroborate this statement.

I would point out, however, that since the doctor has been living in another part of Canada all these years, and the veteran was hospitalized for a long period of time, it is possible that all the details did not appear in the service records.

Then another doctor in the person of Dr. Ritchie is mentioned here. He was questioned as to the possibility of the soldier's being gassed, without any documentary evidence indicating that fact. To this Dr. Ritchie replied that there were many men who did not say anything about it, and that it was his experience that they were not seriously considering the matter at the time. He said:
I know in my hospital experience behind the lines 1 treated a great many with wounds and that sort of thing, who I know had been in gas attacks, and there was no report on their flies.

This veteran has been considered on a number of occasions. He is pensionable for chronic bronchitis with chronic pleurisy, rhinitis and pharyngitis. It is pointed out that the multiple sclerosis is a post-discharge condition not attributable to service. I submit that so little is known about the cause of multiple sclerosis that certainly in my opinion this veteran should be given the benefit of the doubt. He was handled by Dr. Harold in 1917, 38 years ago, and Dr. Harold said he was a stretcher case and was suffering severe pain and weakness in the back and hips, and possibly partial paralysis.

This veteran should certainly be given the benefit of the doubt. I note that in the most recent examination the multiple sclerosis diagnosis has been changed to a diagnosis of osteoarthritis of the spine. I do not know too much about the causes of these particular complaints.

This veteran was also reminded that he had been able to carry on his farming occupation for many years, and that is quite true. I pointed out in my letter to Brigadier Topp that I was convinced that if this veteran had decided in 1919 that he did not want to work it would have been possible for him to have established his right to pension at that time and been a public charge ever since. However, he was an ambitious and loyal citizen, and thought there were things more important than the obtaining of pensions. The fact that he has made a reasonably good living during these years should not be held against him at this time.

On another occasion he travelled from his farm in my riding to the city of Saskatoon to appear before the board. He was asked how he travelled, and he said he had travelled by bus because the train had been cancelled that week due to a bridge washout. One of the examiners suggested that if he were well enough to travel all the way from his farm to Saskatoon by bus he could not be in a very serious condition. This annoyed the veteran very much, because if he had not made the trip he would not have been present for his hearing and his case would not have been reviewed.

I would not have taken the time of the committee had I not felt that this veteran, in his seventieth year, a worthy citizen, should be given the benefit of any doubt, when the fact is that 30 years ago he was a stretcher case; and when one doctor-although it does not appear in the service documents-came to his defence and said that he had examined him, and told what he found. I suggest Dr. Harold's evidence should be given more consideration. It is most unusual for a veteran to be able to discover the doctor who looked after him 35 years ago.

Our pension legislation should be worded so there would not be any doubt at all about a veteran who has this kind of record, so far as having a review of his case is concerned. As he has only a short span of life ahead of him, Canada should be able to give him the benefit of the doubt and decide that because of this unfortunate experience 38 years ago, he should be entitled to pension for this disability for the rest of his life.

The treatment is free provided the adjusted income is below $720. The minister now says it has been increased to $840. The veterans of world war I were entitled to free hospitalization provided that they were classified as indigent. An indigent veteran is one who has an income of less than $1,000.

I see somebody with a look of amazement on his face. That was the definition given to the veterans committee years ago by Dr. Miller. With the value of the dollar today only about 53 per cent of what it was then, why would we lower the amount to $720? That figure should be up around $1,500 to be in line with the rates given to the veterans of world war I. It seems that $720 is altogether too low. 1817947,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.126,1955-07-18,d2512bc7-c1b4-48ab-9772-1abe28ea07fa,ca.m.1774,Mr. Churchill:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,Mr. Chairman, vote 526 deals with the administrative expenses of the Canadian pension commission and is one of the key votes in the series. It affects the following vote 527, which is for almost $130 million for pensions, because the Canadian pension commission is the determining factor in the amount of money that will be paid out for pensions over the year. 1817949,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.128,1955-07-18,unmatched,,,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,First applications to the commission. Of those we granted 490 at the first hearing, and 3,383 were rejected.

As late as this there were that many new applications by world war I veterans. I cannot locate the exact page, but Mr. Melville informed us that of that total of 3,383 applications, 625 were granted and 2,758 were not granted, which indicated that 84 per cent failed in their applications.

There are many things with regard to world war I disability pensions which are interesting and which need examination. I pointed out earlier that of the pensions granted by the pension commission for both wars during the last 12 months, 92 per cent were under the 50 per cent pension scale and only 8 per cent ran from 50 up to 100 per cent. You must realize that if a pensioner is receiving a 50 per cent or higher scale of pension and is married, upon his death his widow automatically becomes entitled to a pension. I am not suggesting at the moment that that fact influenced the pension commission in its findings; it is simply an odd fact to which I draw attention just in passing. I would want to investigate more carefully what has been done up to the present time.

We were interested when discussing this to find the extent to which world war II veterans have benefited from the experience of the pension commission and the veterans of the first world war. In answer to a question which I put, Mr. Melville gave this answer as reported on page 786:

After world war I, a veteran was conceded a pension if he claimed for and established that he had a disability incurred or aggravated during his service. Throughout the years from world war I to world war II, and as a matter of fact up until today, we are still receiving applications for pensions from world war I veterans. When world war II came along, bearing in mind the history of what had happened after world war I, the commission established a very different procedure as follows: we examined the discharge board of every man who served in world war II. If we considered he had a disability at the time of discharge we arranged and called him in for examination, and when we had completed the examination and the other necessary reports we gave a ruling.

So we have apparently benefited from our dealings with world war I veterans, whose documents were not always in very good shape. In one of the letters I mentioned this morning a veteran draws my attention to the fact that although he had been wounded he did not wait to have a medical board at

the time of his discharge in 1919, and did not bother to come before the pension commission until 1932 to disclose his wound and ask for a pension. We can understand some of the reasons why older veterans are appearing at this late date, but I still am surprised at the large number making first applications.

We investigated the method by which applications by world war I veterans are considered, and were informed that there was a first and second hearing followed by an appeal board. I am not going to go into all the details, because we discussed them in the committee, but from what calculations I was able to make I formed the conclusion that your chances of getting a ruling on the first or second hearing were not particularly good. I decided that if I were going to go before the pension commission I would try to get to the appeal board as early as possible, because I found that about 92 per cent of those who had their first and second hearings failed, whereas if a man persisted and got to the appeal board he had a better chance. Your chances on the first and second hearings I judged were about one to twelve, whereas if you got to the appeal board your chance was much better, as about 43 per cent of those appeals were granted.

In view of the earnest desire of the pension commission to settle cases without prolonging them, I have wondered why it has not been possible to get them settled without ending up with an appeal. The commission differs very little in composition in its first and second hearings. The same people are doing the work. Perhaps two would sit on the first hearing and a different two, or maybe three, on the second hearing, and three different commissioners would hear the appeal. But those same three commissioners hearing that particular appeal had perhaps the day before been holding the first hearing on someone else.

I think the appeal board has been built up and magnified in the course of the existence of the pension commission. This is where the minister comes into the picture. I know the pension commission is an independent body, and so on, but when problems of policy arise affecting the actions of the pension commission the minister is the person who would have to arrange for any modification of legislation to help out the commission and at the same time help out the veterans.

That is why we spent some time in that estimates committee discussing the question of the benefit of doubt section. The benefit of doubt section was written into the act chiefly with regard to the problem of world war I veterans who are unable to produce documentary evidence. That is very desirable
Supply-Veterans Affairs

when the commission is sitting on a case. I fully appreciate the value of documentary evidence. It makes it much easier for the commission if it is there, but the documents were not well kept in the first world war. The benefit of the doubt clause, to my mind, was introduced for the express purpose of easing the burden of the pension commission. As you will recall, the benefit of doubt clause says:

Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which means that it is not necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.

Quite a number of veterans feel that the benefit of doubt clause is not invoked. The pension commission people tell me it is invoked in almost every case. There is a wide difference of opinion. My own feeling is that there is some hesitancy about invoking that clause and finding in favour of the veteran without documentary evidence or medical evidence.

The hon. member who preceded me here was speaking some time ago about the effects of poison gas in the first world war. I asked some questions about that in the estimates committee. I am not at all sure that medical opinion could be very definite with regard to an applicant at the present time. The documentary evidence for people gassed during the first world war was often missing. I doubt if many people failed to get a certain amount of poison gas into their lungs, perhaps not to the extent of doing damage, although I have heard medical opinion to the effect that even small amounts of poison gas could result in some damage which would not appear until a great many years had elapsed. The benefit of doubt would be applicable there, I suppose, if an applicant could show that he was in such and such an area at a time of gas shelling, which would take in the greater part of the war. He would surely not have had to be at the battle of Ypres in 1915 to qualify for consideration under that.

That is all I am going to say on that particular section. The pension commission has other duties to perform. It has to deal with cases that arise from people serving now in peacetime, people with the regular army and people in the militia. Here we have run up against very serious trouble. In the estimates committee I asked some questions with regard to section 13(2) and was given the number of people who had made application during the last five years to the pension commission. That is shown on page 875 of the report. The

total number who applied in those five years was 6,952. These would be people who were injured or died during peacetime. Seven hundred and forty-nine were granted while 6,209 were not granted. In other words, 89 per cent of the applicants were not granted a pension because of section 13(2).

Here is where the minister can be of great assistance. He will have to investigate this and find out what can be done toward modifying or altering the legislation under 13(2). I inquired as to whether the pension commission considers a matter like that and puts forward any recommendations concerning a modification of that section. I cannot find the page now, but the information I received was that that was considered by the pension commission and they were trying to evolve some possible modification of that section.

This is serious. This is the section which requires that a person has to show that the disability or death arose out of or was directly connected with such military service. That is the phrase that causes all the trouble. We see the results of these thousands of applications over the last five years under that section. We see how they were refused. I had an experience a few years ago which ended unhappily for the person for whom I was trying to get assistance, and since that time I have been keenly interested in the work of the pension commission. The minister and I do not see eye to eye with regard to this, but two years have gone by since I indicated the effect of that particular section with regard to the death of a certain soldier, and no change has yet been brought about by the minister.

I shall conclude my remarks on this section at that point, because all I am attempting to show is that, valuable and important as is the work of the Canadian pension commission, there are still opportunities for the commission's work to be improved. I think something may well be done by the pension commission to eliminate some of the hardships by getting decisions made prior to reaching the appeal board stage. Something may be done by the minister himself with regard to the benefit of the doubt clause and its application, and with regard to section 13, subsection 2.

If these things are looked at against the background of decisions over the years, I think perhaps some of our veterans, their widows and dependents will receive better treatment than has been accorded them up to the present time. The commission is bound by the act. This is the body which can bring about the necessary changes in the act. I do not think it is in the mind of any member of the House of Commons that widows and
children should suffer because of an act which is not clear as to where responsibility lies when injury or death occurs to members of the services during peacetime.

Of course we are obliged to raise these cases continuously or nothing will be done about them.

The point to which I should like to draw attention is the fact that some applications are turned down on the basis of some pre-enlistment condition. I can understand that situation if it is obvious that it was a pre-enlistment condition, but there is the further fact that many of these men were taken into the forces and given an A-l category on enlistment. Those are the cases which seem to me to be the stickers.

When a man joins the forces and is given a clean bill of health, surely that examination should be thorough enough to make it definite that he is in A-l condition. So he is admitted to the forces. He plays his part. He goes through active service and gives some years of sacrifice to his country. Then as he grows older certain things happen and he has a strong suspicion that they happen by reason of service in the forces. Then, of 50433-401
Supply-Veterans Affairs

course, after examination and after going through all the investigation that doctors and others responsible can go through, the decision is finally arrived at that they cannot grant the pension by reason of some preenlistment ailment which they did not discover when they gave the man a clean bill of health on enlistment.

Naturally the applicant himself is going to be considerably disturbed and agitated. He was perhaps always considered to be in fairly good health as a young man, enlisted and was given a clean bill of health. Now when something is discovered away back there that he did not know anything about, naturally it agitates him considerably because he figures that somebody is ""pulling something"". I am not saying that such men are justified in feeling that way; yet in a sense they are.

I know I cannot urge the matter any more strongly than has been done by my colleagues in all parties who are veterans. I am not a veteran. I had three sons in the war, one of whom gave his life. I am not a veteran myself though I am interested in veterans. But my colleagues who are veterans-some of the first war and some of the second war-and who have been on the veterans affairs committee, know much more about this matter than I do; and they have spoken of it and urged it. As one who is not a veteran but who represents a good many of them, I want to add my voice to those that have been raised in this matter. I feel greatly concerned about that point. I wish the minister could give some expression of opinion as to what might be expected with regard to these regulations.

We are all aware of the fact that the minister himself has done a great deal for the veterans and wants to do more. I do not think any member of the House of Commons has any personal criticism of the minister, his work or his desires. I do not think any of us has any criticism to make of the general work or of the attitude of the pension commission. The regulations are that way. From external appearances, at any rate, it appears that when, under the present regulations, a veteran is refused a pension because of some pre-enlistment condition which he did not know anything at all about, he becomes seriously disturbed.

I do not know whether the minister cares to reply to that statement. I wish he could give us some hope. If he does reply there is something I should like to have. If figures are available, can he tell us this. Of those taken into the forces and given a clean bill of health when they were taken in, how many applicants have been refused pension

1817975,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.154,1955-07-18,d2512bc7-c1b4-48ab-9772-1abe28ea07fa,ca.m.1774,Mr. Churchill:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,"In looking through the

reports over a series of years I, in common with other members of the estimates committee, have wondered how it was possible to estimate so closely the pension requirements for any year. It is a fine piece of calculation indeed. I do not see how the commission can be certain how many people will come up>
and apply for pensions in any year. In fact I would think that in some years there should be double the number of other years.

Astonishingly enough, however, the calculations are pretty accurate. For instance, if one looks into the expenditures for 1952-53 and 1953-54 under the heading ""pensions"" he sees that in the first year the amount was $127,053,000 and in the second it was $127,579,000. Looking at the estimates for 1954-55 we see the amount was $128,030,000 and for 1955-56 it was $129,784,000. Then if we look back at the annual liability as shown in the annual reports of the department and examine the totals for the years 1928 to 1948 for disability pensioners, we discover that in 1928 the annual liability in round figures was $24 million while in 1948 it was $25 million. In between it had gone up to $30 million, and then declined. In 20 years it had gone from $24 million up to $30 million and down to $25 million. This applies only to world war I personnel.

In that same time the number of pensions in force, exclusive of dependents-that is, just the disability pensioners-was 50,635 in 1928 and 69,390 in 1948. In the intervening years the number of pensioners increased to

column2: and declined to 69,000. No matter how one looks at it there appears to be some sort of system over the years whereby pensions would not increase at any alarming rate, and so the total liability would stay about the same. From 1949 to the present date there have been increases in pension rates, and it is difficult to make a comparison, but I shall be watching it with some care in the future.

column1: Supply-Veterans Affairs

It is the greatest piece of calculation I have seen in government circles, and I think the natural course of promotion would be for ministers in the Department of Veterans Affairs to go on to the Department of Finance, because they seem to be able to hit the nail right on the head. Whether they calculate that each year several thousand veterans are going to die and another 3,000 may then come on the pension roll, I do not know. What has struck me in the investigation I have made is that first war pensions should have risen rather sharply in the first ten years, and then declined, and second war pensions it seems to me should do the same, if the system is working accurately. But to have it on a level line, with not much undulation, is a bit odd, to say the least.

1817978,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.8.157,1955-07-18,2b02ca65-52af-436d-9739-c9565c0af670,ca.m.2430,Mr. Lapointe:,Minister of Veterans Affairs,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OP VETERANS AFFAIRS,,The main reason stems from the intention in the act. When the Veterans Land Act was drafted it was proposed that there would be two types of settlement, one for the full-time farmer who would earn his total income from farming operations, and the other for the part-time farmer, the small holder. It was part of the rehabilitation scheme that these small holders would be established on limited acreage, but the idea was that they would be able to supplement their income through making use of the small holdings.

It was found that many would consider establishing themselves as small holders under the Veterans Land Act, not for purposes of rehabilitation but because they wanted to meet a housing need. For that reason it was decided that the small holder would have to acquire a sufficient area of land so he would be able to meet the purpose of the act, which was secondary income through the cultivation of the small holding.

In order to meet the housing demands of veterans on smaller lots or the city-sized lots, we introduced part II of the Veterans Land Act during the course of the last session, and I know my hon. friend is familiar with that particular section.

We are aware that larger amounts were made available last year to both the full-time farmer and the settler going on to the small holding. So far as the full-time farmer is concerned, I believe the larger amount was made retroactive; that is, those who had already been established could make application and could get the larger allowance that was made available. The larger amount was also made available to the small-holding settler. But those who were already established on small holdings did not have this feature of the act made available to them. It would appear that this is something the department could take into consideration, because it looks a little like discrimination. The full-time farmer gets the benefit of it, whereas the man on the small holding does not.

I should like to make the perennial plea on behalf of the old soldier settlers. We know there are still a few of those who after generations, we may say, have not as yet clear title to their property. The amount involved is not much. In fact I understand it would take in the neighbourhood of 2 cents from every person in Canada to wipe out the total indebtedness of the old soldier settlers. I believe no action that might be taken by the department would meet with more favour than if they would consider wiping out this entire debt and give these old veterans clear title to their land.

1817986,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.3,1955-07-18,4cd65efc-8d41-4369-bfc6-0f5452b5f5fd,ca.m.690,Mr. Winters:,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,Mr. Chairman, there were one or two questions outstanding when the committee rose after dealing with these estimates for some time on July 1. As requested by the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) I would be very glad to answer those that seem to be outstanding at the present time.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked first of all about the west block and what our intentions are there. The situation is that the present building is an old one and is badly in need of repair. The repairs will be expensive and will take some considerable time, judging by what is taking place in the parliamentary library at the present moment.

If the building is repaired it will have a useful life of 50 years at the outside. At the same time there is a requirement for a considerable amount of additional space for parliamentary purposes. With that in mind we have asked competent architects to assess the whole situation, to prepare outline plans and specifications, complete with scale models of several alternatives, and then give us an opportunity to look at them, at which time the decision will be made as to what procedure should develop from there.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra also asked whether I would indicate the cost of several typical public buildings in Ottawa. I think he was under the impression that the costs were running high. I have some figures here of typical buildings which indicate that the costs, so far as I know, are pretty well in line with the costs of buildings being erected by private enterprise at the present time.

The east building of the veterans' memorial building on Wellington street cost about $1.27 a cubic foot, about $18.50 a square foot. The west building of the veterans' memorial building is estimated to cost $1.32 a cubic foot, $18 a square foot. The bureau of statistics building in Tunney's pasture cost $1.05 a cubic foot, $18.20 a square foot. The national printing bureau cost 95 cents per cubic foot and $10.82 a square foot. Those are
Supply-Public Works
typical buildings, and I think the figures will show the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that the costs are not out of line.
He then asked about the Marpole bridge in Vancouver, which is a subject we have discussed here on several occasions before. I have nothing further to report since it was last discussed in this house.

The hon. member for York West commented on the type of architecture used in Canadian buildings and suggested that the government should try to encourage a style of typical Canadian architecture, with which I fully agree. I might say that we are now employing a great number of private architects, and in each case they are instructed to design buildings having regard to the Canadian use and try to make them typically Canadian. It would be interesting to note that going into the fiscal year 1954-55 we had 42 architects under contract; during the year we employed another 45, and up to date this year we have employed an additional number that now exceeds 35.

The hon. member for Selkirk questioned the different systems of messing on the dredges operating out of Selkirk, and he made particular reference to the Bradbury. Since the hon. member raised this question I have had the pleasure of visiting Selkirk, talking to the people concerned and seeing some of these boats, particularly the Bradbury. The system of messing is basically the same for all. The difference in the case of the Bradbury, which is a tender and not really a dredge, is that she usually returns to her berth every night and is messed from Selkirk by the department. Another feature is that she has a variable load, in that she carries passengers on the lake in addition to the ordinary complement of crew. On the other hand, the dredges remain away from their bases for long periods of time and the messing is left to the dredge master. In all cases the department pays the same amount in respect to messing, which I believe is $1.53 per man.

The hon. member for Niagara Falls referred several times to the Burlington bridge, as did the hon. member for Halton. I might say that we have drafted an agreement which will enable the federal government to participate in the construction of this bridge to the extent of one-third the estimated cost. The bridge is intended to provide a passage over a canal, which was built by the federal authority, and the federal government therefore feels some responsibility for the bridge. It was estimated that this bridge will cost $13,300,000 and we have told the Ontario government we will pay one-third of that cost. They have been sent a draft agreement,

1817988,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.5,1955-07-18,4cd65efc-8d41-4369-bfc6-0f5452b5f5fd,ca.m.690,Mr. Winters:,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,We have a program of consolidation to bring the architectural staffs together with the engineering staffs and this is part of that process, which I hope will result in greater efficiency.

The hon. member for Eglinton asked if I would say a few words in his absence about the property to which he referred on Wellington street. At the outset I should like to say that although it was clearly defined in Hansard that three properties were involved, the public reading the reports in the press, which generally were quite good, might have formed the opinion that only two properties were involved, that is the Orme and Brock properties, whereas the major portion of the properties involved is the Norlite property which is the biggest and most expensive of the three properties involved.

Perhaps the inference was left that Mr. E. S. Sherwood was acting for the federal government and at the same time was an interested participant in the transaction. Mr. Sherwood was not acting for the federal government, he was acting on behalf of the then owners of the property. Mr. Sherwood had placed a valuation on the properties of $1,646,272.27. As I informed the committee before, we sought the advice of competent independent appraisers to evaluate the property and retained the services of Ernest Pitt and Company, Montreal, and Associated Real Estate Appraisers Inc., also of Montreal. I referred to this company as Appraisers Limited, but this is the correct and full name. Both these appraisers have had comprehensive experience in evaluating properties in Ottawa.

The evaluation arrived at by Associated Real Estate Appraisers Inc. for property and buildings was $1,249,713.32. To that they added $95,437.76 for architects' fees, interest on money, taxes, unforeseen eventualities and so forth, making a total appraised value of $1,345,151.08. In my last statement I omitted this last figure of $95,437.76 as I was dealing only with land and buildings. However, it is an amount that had to be considered in settling for the property.

The Pitt figure for land and buildings was $1,462,863.74. If we add to this the same amount for architects' fees and other expenses that was used in the evaluation by Associated Real Estate Appraisers we reach a total appraisal value of $1,558,301.50. For purposes of comparison with the amount we actually paid it is fair to add architects' and other costs, because we had in fact to pay them in our settlement. In arriving at our final figure we paid $1,396,000, including an allowance for these items.

For purposes of comparison with the appraisals we had there was the figure arising from the Pitt evaluation of $1,558,301.50, including the incidental charges I have referred to already. The Associated Real Estate Appraisers figure was $1,345,151.08 and there was the price requested by E. S. Sherwood of $1,646,272.27, plus 5 per cent interest from the date of expropriation to the date of settlement; and then there was the figure for which we finally settled of $1,396,000.

Before he left the hon. member for Eglinton asked me to indicate the dates on which these appraisals had been submitted. The date of the Ernest Pitt and Company report is January 14, 1954; the date of the report of Associated Real Estate Appraisers is January 18, 1954. Those are the questions the hon. member for Eglinton requested me to answer.
