1817989,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.6,1955-07-18,9fa12394-384b-4e7a-872b-8230b0e27dd7,ca.m.3489,Mr. Winch:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,Under vote No. 1 of the minister's estimates there are three or four matters I should like to raise. Two or three, may I say, are only incidental. One, in my estimation, is rather important. But if I put all the questions in one speech it might expedite the business of this house, so may I just speak on the one or two items which may seem small but which should be drawn to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, because otherwise they might never come to his attention.

All of us in the House of Commons and all residents of Ottawa and, I think I can say, of Canada are very proud of the buildings and grounds of the House of Commons. I was rather amazed to hear that only yesterday, on Sunday, there were over 3,200 visitors taken on conducted tours of the House of
Commons. Therefore the condition of our buildings, our grounds and everything that goes with them should mean a good deal to us.

We speak a great deal about economy. I know this could not have come to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, but I am going to draw it to his attention now. We have in the grounds outside the House of Commons a magnificent iron work as a fence, in particular on the Rideau canal side and going back on the river side. Before I came into politics I was a construction worker, and I have some idea of what that kind of wrought iron work costs.

When I come from where I live, as I have to do every morning, and walk up beside the Rideau canal to the House of Commons and see how that hand-wrought iron work is being allowed to rust and rot because no paint is being put on it to protect it, it breaks my heart. Eventually we are going to have to build a brand new fence there; but why should the Department of Public Works when it is only a matter of spending a few dollars on weather protective paint, allow some of the finest hand-wrought iron in Canada to go to rack and ruin? If I could I would take the Minister of Public Works and show him where it has rusted completely through.

Money means a great deal. Why is the Department of Public Works, which is in charge of our buildings and their surroundings, allowing one of the finest fences in Canada to be ruined because they will not put some paint on it? It is going to cost a good deal of money now even for sandblasting to save it, but I would make the suggestion that the minister tell somebody in his department to go and look at that iron fence and, while they are doing that, to look at the masonry on the Rideau canal side.

On the front of the building you have men working now putting in mortar. You had better start on the Rideau canal side too. The mortar has not only gone on the side but it has gone on the top. Water, snow and ice get in. In Ottawa-not now, but as it was a few months ago-the temperature goes below freezing point and you have blocks that are moving. I just want to say that prevention costs much less than new construction.

As one who worked for years on construction and loves the kind of work we have here, I say, sir, that I know you cannot do it, but you can tell somebody to go and see what is happening to thousands upon thousands of dollars worth of the finest artistry in Canada in our own parliament grounds.
I said I was going to speak very briefly on a few points. I do not know when this house
Supply-Public Works

is going to close, but when it does I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and through you the minister, to do one of two things. Before this house met in the first week of January I understand that somebody exiled a number of cats from the House of Commons. May I suggest that you either bring those cats back or bring exterminators into the House of Commons between sessions and get rid of the mice on the fifth and sixth floors. We did not have them last session. I am amazed that the wives of M.P.'s have not raised particular hell. We now have the problem of mice in room 601. On the sixth floor you can see them going across the floor. There are not only mice in the House of Commons. There are cockroaches in the cafeteria and on the third, fifth and sixth floors of the House of Commons. As I say, it is only a small matter, but it means a great deal.

I suggest that you review the exile of the cats and bring them back or bring in exterminators-not while we are here, but in between sessions-and get rid of the cockroaches and the mice that are invading the building. It is not good advertising, and it is not even nice for the members of the House of Commons to see a mouse all of a sudden dashing across the marble corridors. Mice can do a good deal of damage in a building.

That is all I want to say on that. I just wanted to bring it to the minister's attention that he should take care of the cockroaches and the mice and the painting of the iron rails. It can save a good deal of money if somebody does something about it. I am saying all I wanted to say in one speech, because I want to get home; but I am going to stay here till the bitter end and say whatever I think I should say.

There is a major point that I should like to draw once again to the attention of the Minister of Public Works. I spoke on it last year, and I think it requires that I speak on it again. That is the matter of the highway system of the Dominion of Canada. Arrangements were made whereby the federal government interested itself for the first time in the construction of highways in Canada and reached agreement, I believe, with every province except one on a trans-Canada highway system. As far as I am concerned I want to say thanks for that new policy on behalf of the federal government.

Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that it is necessary that the federal responsibility go further than one trans-Canada highway system. Naturally I have a major interest in the province of British Columbia, which to a great extent is different from the majority
Supply-Public Works

of the provinces of Canada. The province of British Columbia is broken up north and south by four main mountain ranges. There are only three passes east and west. We have the Crowsnest pass in the south. We have the Kicking Horse pass or the Big Bend which is accepted now as the trans-Canada route. North of that, and where we have no roads at all, we have the Yellowhead pass.

Those hon. members who come from the prairies and from the other provinces do not realize the cost of highway construction with which we are faced in British Columbia. If my memory serves me correctly the average cost of a highway on the prairies, up to the standards laid down by the federal government on the trans-Canada highway, is about $45,000 a mile. In British Columbia we have spots that cost us $1 million a mile; and that is not just an occasional mile.

I know that under the trans-Canada highway contract the federal government will pay half that cost. But, Mr. Chairman, that affects only one highway in British Columbia. Again I want to ask the Minister of Public Works whether he will not give consideration to a new policy of highway construction. The government has already accepted the principle of a financial interest in highway construction; it has been accepted by every province except one. But that is only on what is known as the trans-Canada highway; that is only on one highway across Canada. I suggest to the minister that the federal authority accept a financial responsibility and a planning responsibility not just with regard to one highway across Canada but with regard to every primary highway in every province of Canada.

Primary highways open up new industries, new developments and new resources. The major beneficiary of new developments and new resources is the federal treasury through all its taxes. I know that a province should accept its responsibility. A province should invest its money in developing its resources. But because we in our dominion are a federal state I say the federal government should also accept some responsibility for financial investment in the provinces because the federal treasury will reap a major benefit from that development; and one of the finest things for development is the opening up of the country by a major primary highway system.

I am a citizen of the city of Vancouver, which has about a third of the entire population of the province of British Columbia. At the moment we have only one highway system that is recognized by the federal government, and that is Kingsway on the trans-Canada highway. We have two other outlets from the city of Vancouver going

east. However, I do not think the one on Burrard inlet can ever be developed as a major road. We have one other outlet which goes straight through the heart of Vancouver and north of New Westminster. I refer to the Lougheed highway.
There are a few more words that I should like to say about this matter, Mr. Chairman. May I ask you to call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

I was discussing a most important matter, and I should like to continue in the hope the minister could give some assurance that the subject will be considered. It is not enough to think that Canada, being a federated country, has a national highway policy when the federal government makes an agreement and contributes to one highway on a trans-Canada basis. The United States is also a federated country, with 48 states, and the federal government there recognizes that an investment in primary highways is a good investment for the national government. I say, sir, it is also a good investment for the national government of Canada.

In Canada we have a country with marvellous resources. Directly and indirectly the federal government reaps a great benefit to the national treasury through the development of natural resources. One of the finest ways of furthering the development of new resources and the establishment of new industries, is through the medium of highway development. In British Columbia-and naturally I have a keen interest in that province because I represent a constituency there-we have a problem that no other province in Canada has because of our four mountain ranges running from north to south.

I want to say, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the Minister of Public Works, that I doubt if there is any province in Canada from which the federal government gets a greater per capita return to the national treasury than it gets from British Columbia. I know that British Columbia pays more income taxes than Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba put together. I am not being at all critical of those provinces, but I am pointing out the return the federal government gets from British Columbia. We have major problems connected with highways, and I believe the minister will eventually have to come to a national highway policy and accept responsibility in all provinces for major primary highways, not just the trans-Canada highway.

I know that British Columbia would like to be able to meet her commitments on the trans-Canada highway and complete it. But, sir, we have other major highway responsibilities in British Columbia. We cannot expend all the money British Columbia has available on one 30433-402
Supply-Public Works

highway. You have to come to it eventually, and the sooner you come to it the sooner the federal government is going to increase its revenue. The sooner we have a national policy of assisting all provinces not merely on one route across the province but on all primary highways, the better it will be not only for the provinces but for Canada as a whole.

This is a subject upon which I could speak for hours. It is close to my heart. I know that eventually we shall come to it, so why not now? At least the minister should inform this house and the provinces that he has under consideration a plan of assistance for all provinces in their primary highway construction, and in particular British Columbia because I am a member from that province and I know its problems. We now have our southern route in the Crowsnest, but we are blocked in two ways, one over the Cascade mountains. Personally I believe our route should not be over the Cascade mountains at all on the southern route, but the federal government should get us a corridor in the United States by means of which we could completely avoid spending millions of dollars crossing the Cascade mountains. I have gone over the route; I know it is practical and that it is undeveloped in the United States.

The province alone cannot handle a project of that kind. We have the Big Bend, the Kicking Horse pass route, which is the trans-Canada route; but the Mica dam is going to go in some day and, when it does, no less than 32 miles will be flooded. Then there will have to be a complete rerouting. We have the Yellowhead pass route, which is not yet built. In my estimation it is a good one, and has been proven by the Canadian National Railways to be a good one. They go through on the Yellowhead pass and do not even need pushers on their freight trains.

Those are our routes, our only means of ingress and egress. We cannot spend all our money on the trans-Canada highway. We can develop British Columbia to an even greater extent than it is being developed today if we can obtain some help from the federal government, which should be vitally interested. But until now it has not spent any money. I say to this government that if it wants returns it must also make investments.

Has the Minister of Public Works given any consideration to a national highway program in Canada, beyond the trans-Canada route, in which it will invest in the development of the provinces by assisting them in their program of primary highway development? If they did, then the provinces could spend their money on the secondary feeders

into those primary routes. That is a logical development, and one that would pay dividends to the provinces, and most certainly to the federal government. Has the minister anything of that nature in mind, and will he comment on the matter?

1818002,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.19,1955-07-18,4cd65efc-8d41-4369-bfc6-0f5452b5f5fd,ca.m.690,Mr. Winters:,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,I agree with the hon. member that the part he mentioned earlier is not in as good state of repair as we would like to have it. But that work will be undertaken shortly, and we have every intention of maintaining that fence.

Then with regard to the mice and cockroaches, as I said earlier that is a matter of housekeeping which comes under the jurisdiction of His Honour the Speaker, and I am sure he is quite competent to deal with it.

Then, as to highways, I think the hon. member will agree with me that our first aim and object must be to complete the trans-Canada highway. Here I would remind hon. members of the committee that nine of the ten provinces signed agreements with us to complete their work on the trans-Canada highway by December 9, 1956. For a variety of reasons that work has lagged. In the three western provinces it has lagged because of weather conditions. I had the opportunity last week of driving over a portion of the highway between Maple Creek and Medicine Hat, and I saw again how impossible it is to do highway work on the western prairies under conditions of wet weather. They have made a good effort, however, and I hope they will carry on.

As of today the total contractual commitments for the trans-Canada highway amount to $193,406,067.61, of which the federal government is committed to half. To date the federal government has actually paid

$66,108,982.38. In addition the federal government assists with other highways and development roads; and as hon. members know, the federal government is entirely and fully responsible for all highways in the northern territories.

The hon. member spoke about the United States effort. Our effort in Canada, on a per capita basis, does not suffer too much in comparison with the United States. It must be remembered, too, that in that country they have a federal tax on gasoline which yields annually something of the order of $1,500 million, which is considerably in excess of what the federal government has been spending on highways there. In this country we have no such revenue.

I agree entirely with what the hon. member said about the value of highways in the development of the country. We are continually thinking in terms of what might be done in the future to stimulate and assist development, always having in mind our immediate objective, that of completing the trans-Canada highway.

Hon. members know that we have on the agenda for the federal-provincial conference this fall the subject of public investment, and I would not be at all surprised if participation in the provincial highways program were one of the subjects discussed there.

1818007,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.24,1955-07-18,ea30e79d-1feb-461a-bbea-b3e5a570ee30,ca.m.468,Mr. Nowlan:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,I would like to come back to the ground on which we are now standing. The minister told us this afternoon that no decision had been made, as I understood him, with respect to the west block. He said he had asked for plans to be prepared and that there might be renovation, or that there might be reconstruction, or that there might be construction of a new building.

I noticed in one of the newspapers-I believe it was the Montreal Gazette-that someone in his department said that so far there had been only one protest received respecting the demolition of the west block. If only one protest has been received up to now, then I would like to increase the protests by 100 per cent by registering a
Supply-Public Works
second one. Personally I feel it would be a serious mistake to have the west block destroyed or torn down, or even to have an exact replica of it constructed in its place.

Obviously there have been leaks-perhaps inspired leaks, I think-in this matter. We have read that it would cost $6 million for a new building and $3 million to renovate the old one, and there has been a great deal of speculation. I was very glad indeed to hear the minister say this afternoon that no decision had been made, that he was asking for reports and for the preparation of plans, and that after he had that background material he would make a decision on the basis of the information available to him.

I commend him for that. My own personal opinion at the moment is that whatever the dollar cost of building may be, as represented by the plans he receives, the minister should decide that the present building must be maintained. After all, Mr. Chairman, I think we are engaging here in one of the most interesting experiments that has ever been carried on in any country in the world. We are trying to evolve a Canadian nation in this country, based first on two distinctly different racial groups. With that background we are bringing in hundreds of thousands, and we hope millions, of people of other races and other outlooks. Out of that amalgam we are creating a distinctive Canadian nation. I ask you, how are you going to do it if you intend to tear down and destroy-for the sake of getting fluorescent lighting or elevator service, or nice pink and green walls, or something of that kind-the very basis on which this nation was constructed?

Actually on this hill here we have the two old buildings, the east block and the west block. We had the old centre block, which was destroyed by fire and which has been replaced by this building, the centre of the original government of Canada. I hope a hundred years from now Canadians will be coming here and looking over this hill and saying, ""There was the establishment of government of Canada; that is where they first met. There is the east block and the west block"". Tonight we are sitting in the building which takes the place of the one which was destroyed by fire.

It is true that the west block is an old building and probably needs extensive repairs. I can feel sorry for those who work in it. They would like to have all sorts of modern innovations and improvements, and they probably deserve them. After all, Mr. Chairman, we are erecting buildings around this city very rapidly. A tremendous number of government buildings are going up all over the place. Although one does not wish to 50433-402J
encourage the spending of money, there are certain aesthetic things one can speak of, and one of them is the maintenance of national traditions and historic centres.

This year the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources introduced legislation to enlarge the national historic sites and monuments board. That board is to preserve the historic sites of this country. What would it think, what would the people of Canada think, if we authorize or permit, without at least registering a protest, the responsible minister in charge of the buildings here to tear down and destroy one of the historic landmarks of this nation? I am sure that in Washington, for instance, pressure has been brought to bear on the government to tear down old buildings and replace them with new ones. I am sure that in London there is just as much demand for space and for real estate as there is here.

I have forgotten my history, but it seems to me that No. 10 Downing street was erected by Sir Charles Downing somewhere around 1650, or between that and 1700. It is still preserved as the home of the British prime minister, and is actually the seat of the British cabinet. Westminster hall was built long before that. There undoubtedly were pressures brought to bear to tear out the floors and the lighting and put in fluorescent lighting and put up a modern structure, but they resisted that. In Philadelphia, Independence hall-and I am sure real estate is as valuable there as it is here-was preserved and the great park in front of it was preserved as an historic shrine to the establishment of the American government. Surely we can do as much here.

I am not going to take any more time of the committee, Mr. Chairman. Like the hon. member who preceded me, I feel fairly strongly on this matter. I could speak at length. I speak to the minister as a responsible minister of this government, and I also speak to him as a personal friend, I hopfe, when I say that building should not be torn down and destroyed. You can say you can build an exact replica, and you can do it for $6 million. We have seen these estimates. It will cost $18 million before they get through with it, and it will be no more like the present building than day is like night.

A hundred years from now, if this nation survives and develops in the way we are trying to develop it, people will be coming to Ottawa and looking around and asking, where is the west block? The answer will be, that was destroyed while Bob Winters was Minister of Public Works. If that happens it will not add greatly to his reputation. I say that

as a friend. I ask him to study this very carefully and to weigh the aesthetic values against dollars and cents, if that is possible in this day and age. If he does that I am quite certain he will come to the decision that the west block should be preserved. If so, Canada will be the better because of it.

I wish I had been more explicit when I raised the grievance on the floor about those fellows who get $1.54 a day for their meals. I think that runs to about $47 a month. I also referred to two dredges. The grievance is that on the Bradbury the $47 is paid for every man who eats, but on the dredges they do not need to spend the $47, as they do on the other boat. Some individual in the crew buys the food, and if they have a crew of ten and they spend only $400, the other $70 does not go back into the kitty; it does not go back into the consolidated revenue fund. Somebody gets it.

The argument of the men on the dredge is that they should be fed in the same way as the men are fed on the Bradbury. The minister tonight gave one or two instances to show that it was not very convenient, but I think it can be done. I am going to ask him again to see what he can do about having the men employed by the same department fed in the same way, and then there will be no hard feelings. I have been at sea long enough to know that it is terrible when you have a dissatisfied crew. They are dissatisfied about their food. If they are not getting the food they should be getting the $47 a month and nothing less.
I spoke on these estimates before, Mr. Chairman. I talked about the breakwater at Gimli. That was on July 1. The minister interrupted to say, as reported at page 5582 of Hansard:
There was supposed to be fill behind it, put there by the municipality. The fill was never put there. That is why the breakwater washed away.

It would take longer than from now to ten o'clock to read all the letters I have received in connection with these few remarks. I hold in my hand a telegram from the Gimli chamber of commerce. It reads:
Have written Minister of Public Works and copy to you good photos of cracks in Gimli breakwater forwarded to minister today.
I hope the minister got those photographs because they will give him an idea of how serious the situation is. The mayor of Gimli writes as follows:

I do not know why the minister would say that the breakwater is washed away because we, the town of Gimli, did not fill behind it, as you know this is not true. I do not think there is any part of the breakwater that was not backfilled. I will admit that there may be places where not enough backfill was placed, but where the breaks in the breakwater have occurred the cause has not necessarily been the lack of fill.

Also please remember that each property owner had to sign and assume the responsibility of backfilling behind their own property which made it very difficult for the town of Gimli to interfere with those particular ratepayers.

And also when this breakwater was constructed a tremendous amount of rock had been placed along the shoreline by these people and the town of Gimli. This material was simply used by the government for the construction of the breakwater.

As I stated earlier I do not think that there is any portion of the breakwater that has not been backfilled, most of it excellently done, but of course you will realize that after two or three years a certain amount of sagging has taken place.
Please convey to the minister from me that, if this is the information he gets from his engineers, he needs a new engineer.

I think I once pointed out to you how this breakwater was built, particularly the most southerly portion where the town joins the municipality. This as I think you know is crumbling due to poor construction and I shall defy any engineer to tell me different. On a separate piece of paper I shall draw you a sketch of this portion to refresh your memory.
I shall take that up with the minister later. Then the Gimli chamber of commerce wrote to the minister under date of July 6. The pertinent parts of this letter read:

A great deal of rock was hauled by volunteers and by the town of Gimli to the breakwater site. This was originally intended to serve as backfill when the new breakwater was built. However, much of this was used in the actual construction of the breakwater. It is true that the town had the responsibility of backfill and maintenance. And in every case where town property meets the breakwater this has been backfilled. It is also true that there are homes that have not adequately backfilled their properties that adjoin the breakwater, but on the other hand regions that have been properly backfilled are among those that have suffered the greatest damage.
Supply-Public Works

We are unanimous in our conviction that the damage to the breakwater is due to faulty construction. As enclosed photographs will demonstrate, one residence which has a solid rock and concrete backfill behind the breakwater is in great danger because this precaution has not prevented large cracks from occurring in the breakwater. This home owner testifies that the asphalt at this point is breaking loose in large chunks.

Where the government ditch enters the lake at the municipal-town boundary there is evidence of very poor engineering. Here the lake has just crumbled the breakwater. Please refer to large photograph enclosed.

The Gimli chamber of commerce takes exception to the statement that adequate backfill would have prevented crumbling of the breakwater. These photos show cracks where adequate backfilling has been carried out. We feel that the engineers that reported to you in this matter are in error.

Those are some of the things the chamber of commerce have to say. I am not going to take up much more time of the committee because there are many estimates to be dealt with, but here is what John Arnason, an old resident of Gimli, has to say:
Dear Mr. Bryce.

There is no doubt about the construction of the government wall at Gimli being faulty. They made it too solid, not allowing the overrun to flow back. They should have had openings to let the water run back, that is the whole trouble. I own 180 feet fronting the wall. It collapsed this summer as the backrun was too strong. South of the government wall I have 100 feet where I built my own and it is still standing as it was made to have the water run back as fast as it came over. I asked the municipality men here who has to look after government wall. They said the porperty owners. When the wall was first built I had bought stones to protect the 180 feet shoreline. I was never allowed one cent for same. Now to protect myself and I feel all the settlement behind I bought $260 stones that I have piled behind the government wall to hold it from flattening out. Another thing, the government wall was only cemented in the front. All the back was only loose stones piled up. The back-wash washed them out and then no support. Our best breakwaters are large stones that don't wash away, but they cost money, $10 per load, but should we on the waterfront protect all the others living behind? Who should I go to that will share the cost?

That man has lived there all his life and he claims it was faulty, that there should be holes in the wall to allow the water to run back. I appeal to the minister to have his engineers do something about this. There are a lot of nice people in Gimli and I have to go back there to live among them. If you do not do something about the breakwater it is going to be too bad for me. The funny thing about this breakwater is that when I represented this community about eight years ago the government said it was not their responsibility. Then after redistribution they were able to get a Liberal member, and the government then found that it was their responsibility. I can show articles in the local newspapers where it is stated that the Department of Public Works assumed responsibility which they never knew they
had before. It was found they had built a wooden breakwater years ago. I appeal to the minister to do something.

1818012,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.29,1955-07-18,87d8cf85-54d0-4c2b-9e84-5c3d33a1a514,ca.m.6621,Mr. Dickey:,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer for a moment to the remarks made a short time ago by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in connection with the west block. I believe all of us in this chamber have an appreciation of the traditions of this country and the necessity of maintaining historic landmarks and that sort of thing. However, I think both this committee and the country must recognize that we are faced with a practical problem and it is the Minister of Public Works who has the responsibility of solving that problem.

The problem is to provide necessary space for the essential services of this parliament, and I think everything that is done should be done with the primary objective in mind of meeting properly the essential requirements of members of both houses of this parliament and the people who serve our needs. The question of the preservation of the west block I think has to be looked at first of all in that light.

After listening to the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings it is quite clear that he himself destroyed his own argument by reference to this centre block in which we meet. He described the original building, which was of the kind and type of the west block and the east block and was destroyed by fire.

What was the result of that fire? The result of that fire was that there was built here on this site what I think is certainly the most beautiful and the most efficient government building I have ever seen, and one of the finest government buildings in any capital in the world. It is not a building that the hon. member or any other member of this house can say does not preserve and pay tribute to the original design of this parliament hill and the traditional feeling of this country, but it is an immeasurably more appropriate, more useful and more adequate building than the old one ever was.

only now started drafting sketch plans, and they have put nothing concrete before us. I read what my colleague the Minister of Defence Production said about his own program, and I have no disagreement about that. 1818042,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.59,1955-07-18,fdce9d46-5c36-4ca6-b6c7-52d1e6f9ba0b,ca.m.8192,Mr. Low:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,I wanted to take just a very few minutes to ask the minister about two matters of policy. Briefly the matter which was raised by the hon. member for New Westminster, and which he asked me to remind the minister about since he is now overseas on this NATO

tour, is a question concerning the policy of the Department of Public Works with respect to the construction of buildings on the one hand or rental on the other. I believe the hon. member for New Westminster outlined some specific examples to the Minister of National Defence and also quoted from newspaper articles with respect to a specific building in the city of Vancouver. The question that was asked was, does the minister feel he is justified in renting buildings when the amount of rental he pays will return to the owners the full value of the building in seven years or less?

With respect to our rental of buildings, we act almost entirely through the Department of Public Works. I understand there are appraisers who fix the values. The hon. member for New Westminster has also had a number of questions on the order paper, two of which I believe were answered today. I have not had an opportunity of looking at those answers. They might contain the very information I should like to have, and perhaps when the minister does reply he could give us the substance of the replies that have been prepared. At any rate I should like to have the government policy with respect to rentals or construction, and where the line is drawn in their decision to do one or the other.

The second matter I wanted to raise was this. I believe the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources received today -if he has not he will receive in the next day or two-a letter and resolution from the associated boards of trade of the Peace river country relative to the Mackenzie highway. A copy of that letter was sent to me. I have read the resolution, and as a result I wanted to ask the minister to give me some idea of the government's present policy with respect to sharing the costs with provincial governments of roads that lead into the Northwest Territories, and over which much heavy equipment is now being moved for the development of the north country.

I might refresh the minister's memory by telling him that about 18 years ago the government of Alberta did push through a winter road, a tractor road, from Grimshaw in the Peace river country to Great Slave lake down on the Hay river. That is a distance of approximately 200 miles. The following spring
Supply-Public Works
the government oi Canada joined with the government of Alberta and together they built the road that is now known as the Mackenzie highway, servicing that whole northern country.

Since that time, of course, there has been a tremendous development all along the road. I might also say to the minister that since the first road was built, the cost of which was shared by both governments, the provincial government has spent more in improving that road than the original cost. Today I doubt that there is a busier highway in the whole of western Canada than the highway from Grimshaw to Great Slave lake, because over it is being carried the great bulk of heavy equipment and supplies required in the tremendous development of the Northwest Territories.

As the minister probably knows, in the spring of the year when the frost goes out, the roads in the northern country become soft and, as a consequence, the government of the province which must administer the regulation of traffic on the highway will either have to place a ban on the hauling of heavy loads, or they will have to let the trucks go through and be prepared to rebuild the road in a very few years. Today the traffic is so heavy, and it is so essential that materials get through on time, that I am of the opinion development will be retarded unless there can be worked out some close co-operation between the two governments to see that the road is built to a standard that will carry the heavy traffic.

As the minister knows, when progress is made in the building of a new road, then almost immediately truckers will put on box cars. They are more than keeping up with the new construction devised to have the roads stand up. These heavy loads go in there and, of course, tear the roads to pieces. The great bulk of the traffic consists of material going in for the development and expansion of the great north country.

I would ask the minister to state the policy of this government with respect to sharing the cost of such road building and improvement, and I would ask him to state if he would consider joining with the provincial government in making improvements on the Mackenzie highway so traffic can go on through unimpeded during the whole season, in order that progress in the Northwest Territories may continue.

In closing I would point out it is expected that in the general area of Alberta within the next few years the provincial government hopes to open up somewhere in the neighbourhood of two million acres more of land to homesteaders, so the population of the country will push farther and farther to the north.

Great farming areas will develop all through that northern area, and doubtless tributary to the highway towns and villages will spring up. I am wondering if some arrangement could be worked out in close co-operation so a permanent highway that would stand up under heavy traffic could be built and maintained by the two governments.

1818043,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.60,1955-07-18,4cd65efc-8d41-4369-bfc6-0f5452b5f5fd,ca.m.690,Mr. Winters:,Minister of Public Works,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,The hon. member's first question had to do with our policy of rentals, and an indication of where the breaking point is when we make a decision to rent as against constructing a building, or vice versa. The reply is that we consider each case carefully before deciding whether we should build or enter into a rental agreement. It is not only the cost of the rental that must be considered. When we build a new building we have to assume the responsibility for its operation, which usually includes cleaning staff, janitor service, lighting and so on. For these relatively small properties, in most cases the terms of the leases provide that the owners supply janitor service, cleaning, heat, light and the other incidental services, all of which we would have to provide, at the cost of money and personnel, if we were to build our own building.

I think the hon. member will also note that in the circumstances he has in mind the leases almost invariably go back a number of years. In one case it has been outstanding since 1947, and in others since the early fifties. I can assure him that we do look carefully into all these cases to determine whether we should rent or build.

The other point he raised had to do with highways, and particularly the Mackenzie highway. I am not sure what the policy of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is now, but when I was responsible for the department of resources and development we assumed full responsibility for the maintenance of that portion of the highway between the 60th parallel and Hay river. I am sure I can say for my colleague the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that it is the government's intention to keep that road in adequate shape to carry any type of highway traffic that can reasonably expect to use it.

I know the hon. member is well aware that there is another great development road passing through Alberta over part of its course, for which the federal government has assumed full responsibility. I am referring of course to the northwest highway.

There are no facilities for landing tourists from their motor boats.

1818057,ca.proc.d.1955-07-18.1.9.74,1955-07-18,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Mr. Drew:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS,,I simply want to mention briefly the subject that has been already under discussion, namely the west block and the possibility of the construction of a new building there, or substantial changes to the present building.

Following the remarks of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, the senior member for Halifax said we must be practical. I think we must be practical. One of the ways in which we can be most practical is to realize that if we are going to develop the spirit of the nation we must preserve some of the visible symbols of the development of this nation. We have also within the grounds of parliament hill one unique reminder of the early association of Ottawa with the formation of Canadian government. It is not simply a sentimental thing, it is a most practical thing.

I think one of the reasons Westminster has stayed as an example to the whole world of the priceless value of continuing tradition is that they have not too readily destroyed the evidence of the past. There are many hon. members here, including the minister, who have been in the halls of Westminster
in which the whole story of British history has been formed, going back some 800 years. It might have been practical in the cold meaning of that word to have a more modern building.

There is need for modern accommodation here and I think we should have much more modern accommodation. Land is becoming increasingly expensive in Ottawa, but it is still relatively cheap as compared with land in the heart of London. Nevertheless they have preserved the buildings, some of them going back 600, 700 and 800 years. They have done this not simply as a reminder of the past but because they are part of the continuing love of British tradition. We in Canada should retain the opportunities we have to preserve the Canadian tradition of parliament. This is one unique opportunity. In many ways it is of more value from the historical point of view than this building itself.

I do not believe there are any demands sufficiently compelling from the practical point of view to justify the destruction of that historic building and to remove permanently those offices which carry the memories of the spirit of great men who did much to mould this nation. Those were men of both political parties which have shared the responsibilities of government. Their memories should be honoured, and this is one way it can be done rather than to merely say that the architects will be called upon to prepare plans and a decision will be made. I would hope that from the grounds of high practical considerations and the value of our own history a decision would be made that the west block will be preserved in order that people will be able to go there and see the places where men have played their part in moulding the nation.

Not long ago a number of us were privileged to be present when Sir Archibald Nye, the high commissioner for the United Kingdom, presented a remarkable photographic record of Earnscliffe which has been identified with Canadian history in a manner which most hon. members will recall, particularly the fact that it was once the home of Sir John Macdonald. At that time the Prime Minister and others emphasized the value of preserving these historic traditions. Naturally I would subscribe to any effort made to preserve the historical associations of Sir John Macdonald, but in saying that I do not suggest for a moment that my Liberal friends opposite would not subscribe also to the same purpose and idea.
The Prime Minister emphasized the value of efforts of this kind. If it is worth while
Supply-Public Works

to preserve by photographs the living history of buildings in this area such as Earnscliffe, surely it is worth while to preserve intact the building where so much of the actual business of government was done in days gone by.

But to say that the whole interior of the building must be preserved in its present form is just neither logical nor consistent. It is quite true that there was a most interesting ceremony here some weeks ago with reference to the home of the first prime minister of Canada, but when the Leader of the Opposition was recognizing that fact I could not help thinking that prime minister would be the first to be progressive and enterprising enough to know that something substantial had to be done with the office building which is unfortunately located on parliament hill, known as the west block, and that his wishes would have been that it be brought in line with the functions it served when he occupied it as prime minister, and also that it be brought in line with the functions it now serves.

There is only a small part of the building that has historical significance. I do not want to get diverted, but there was the prime minister's office, a staircase and so on. That should be preserved. While having the utmost respect for the historical associations, I think we owe it to the citizens of Canada to apply our reasoning and logic to these things.
